topic: 4x DGX Sparks: the rack, power and multi-node math
title: Four DGX Sparks Buy Memory, Not Speed
description: One DGX Spark holds one hundred twenty-eight gigabytes. Four, cabled in a ring, hold a model no single GPU can load. Here is what it buys.
hook_text: Your DGX Spark just hit its ceiling.
hook_candidates: Your DGX Spark just hit its ceiling.
Four thousand seven hundred dollars a box. Four boxes.
Five hundred twelve gigabytes. No GPU you can buy has that.
Four Sparks bought memory, not speed.
One box is a toy. Four are a rack.
You bought one hundred twenty-eight gigabytes. The biggest models laugh at it.
A team bought four DGX Sparks. Here is the math.
Why would anyone cable four Sparks in a ring?
The cable, not the box, decides your speed.
Your rack reads at human pace. That is the point.
narration_full: Your DGX Spark just hit its ceiling. The newest open models grew past what your box can hold. An open model called GLM five point two just landed. Its card lists seven hundred fifty-three billion parameters, the stored dials a model reads to write. No single graphics card you can buy holds them all. Your Spark carries one hundred twenty-eight gigabytes of unified memory, one pool the processor and the graphics chip share. That was roomy last year. This model is roomier. So you cable four Sparks together. Tensor parallelism, the trick that splits one model across boxes, pools their memory into one heap. Four boxes give five hundred twelve gigabytes of pooled memory, and the giant finally fits. Here is the catch, straight from Petronella's measurements. Inside a box, memory feeds the chip over a wide road. The cable between boxes is about a tenth as wide. Every word pulls some weights through it. Picture four movers with one piano. Together they lift it, but they keep stopping to call out the next step. A benchmark team called Petronella ran four boxes on GLM five point three Flash, a smaller open model. On plain prose it decoded twenty-six point five tokens per second. A token is a chunk of a word, so that is reading pace. The piano picture bends for sparse models like Qwen three point eight Flash Next, a kind that wakes only a few small specialists per word. There, more boxes really do pay. Alex Ellis's team built this. They cabled four Sparks into a closed ring, with no network switch at all. They also patched the networking library that moves data between boxes, so neighbors relay. So what did four boxes buy? Not speed. The decode strolls at reading pace. They bought a model class your shelf could not hold yesterday. Four Sparks buy memory, not speed. The model that outgrew your one box now fits on four, and it answers at the pace you read.

analogy.mapping: One consumer GPU is a strong lone mover: quick on its feet, but a seven hundred fifty-three billion parameter piano will not fit on its back. Four Sparks are four ordinary movers who can carry it together, except they keep stopping to call out and coordinate, which is the thin cable between the boxes.
analogy.limit: The picture bends for expert-mixture models, where each box's share of the work per word shrinks and four boxes can beat two.

notes_for_review: Check that the twenty-six point five tokens per second stays glued to GLM five point three Flash and never leaks onto the seven hundred fifty-three billion parameter model, whose four-node speed is unverified in the brief. The phrase 'about a tenth as wide' derives from two seven three versus twenty-five gigabytes per second, which this draft may not speak, so confirm that qualitative framing is acceptable. 'Just landed' for GLM five point two rests on the Ellis post being hours old; soften to 'recently' if the air date slips.
